claims.title: From cells to the global inequality

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: The seven arguments of `CellSystemCondition` must be interpreted together, because the cell layouts, tree and assembly records are typed over the preceding data.

anchor.heading: The seven inputs must describe one instance

comparisons.note: The condition applies to seven linked collections of data and requires all fifteen groups of geometric, analytic and numerical assumptions for that same instance.
The basic data fix the certificate, weights, frozen profile, physical cells, polynomial fields, pins and actuator information used throughout the construction.
The instance data attach the weights, frame rates, support information and row bounds to the previously chosen cell problem.
The cell calculation uses the chosen layouts, local forms and assembly matrices on resolved data, ports and both actuator blocks.
The tree data use the same global coordinates and cell matrices, with specified fronts, pivots, loss columns, gauge directions and admissible base points.
The assembly data provide the coupling, omitted-mode, exterior and row information for the same cells and global coordinates.
The four stored numbers are the two multiplier error bounds, the velocity-piece ratio bound and the global error allowance used by this instance.
The reduction data supply the represented profile, pressure, adjoints, potentials and numerical bounds for the parameter and adjoint estimates.

comparisons.note: The conversion sends the lattice label ι to the frequency pair (2ι₂−ι₁, κι₁), exactly as stated.
The temporal integer attached to ι is 2ι₂−ι₁, the first component of the stated frequency pair.
The azimuthal integer attached to ι is κι₁, the second component of the stated frequency pair.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: Reflection sends the lattice label to $(-\iota_1,\iota_2-\iota_1)$, whereas the corresponding physical pair $(j,n)$ goes to $(j,-n)$.

anchor.heading: Coordinates, harmonics and normalisation

comparisons.note: Reflection sends ι to (−ι₁,ι₂−ι₁), preserving its temporal frequency and reversing its azimuthal frequency.
On physical frequency pairs the reflection is (j,n)↦(j,−n), consistent with the stated reflection of lattice labels.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: A field key includes a further integer $\ell$ for radial phase.

anchor.heading: Coordinates, harmonics and normalisation

comparisons.note: A harmonic key consists of the lattice label and a further integer specifying the radial phase multiple.
The full factor is exp(i(2πjθ+nφ+ℓf(ρ²))), so the radial phase uses the additional integer ℓ.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: Negation of a key changes both $\iota$ and $\ell$; reflection changes $\iota$ and retains $\ell$.

anchor.heading: Coordinates, harmonics and normalisation

comparisons.note: Conjugation negates both the lattice label and its radial phase integer, as required to negate the entire oscillatory phase.
Reflection changes the lattice label and leaves the radial phase integer unchanged.
The finite support is completed under conjugation and reflection by taking the original keys and their three corresponding images.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: The constructor `reducedComps` enforces divergence freedom algebraically in each harmonic.

anchor.heading: The divergence-free profile representation

comparisons.note: The nonzero azimuthal modes reconstruct the third component algebraically from two amplitudes; the zero mode uses the stream and swirl representation with its origin correction.
The radial derivative includes the phase derivative term iℓf′ times the amplitude; this is the term needed in the harmonic divergence cancellation.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: Each profile spline has its own product mesh in $[0,1]\times[-1,1]$.

anchor.heading: Splines and jets

comparisons.note: The mesh condition requires strictly increasing radial and polar knots with endpoints 0,1 and −1,1, respectively.
The spline condition imposes polynomial edge identities through the specified derivative orders on a full radial and polar mesh.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: Spline evaluation assigns an internal knot to the interval on its right, while the final endpoint remains in the last interval; `cellIndex` implements this by counting internal knots below or equal to the coordinate.

anchor.heading: Splines and jets

comparisons.note: Counting interior knots less than or equal to the coordinate assigns a knot to its right interval, while the final endpoint remains in the last interval.
Evaluation first selects the intervals by that knot rule and then evaluates their polynomial at the chart coordinates.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: Integer temporal harmonics provide period-one dependence; the radial and polar spline endpoints are not identified periodically.

anchor.heading: Splines and jets

comparisons.note: The represented field has integer temporal harmonics, exact conjugation and reflection identities, prescribed spline joins, endpoint orders and origin cancellations.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: A radial phase is $C^3$ on a neighbourhood of the nonnegative axis, with bounded $x f'(x)$, $x^2f''(x)$ and $x^3f'''(x)$.

anchor.heading: Splines and jets

comparisons.note: The phase is C³ on an open interval containing [0,∞), and x f′, x²f″ and x³f‴ have common uniform bounds there for x≥0.
The sentence concerns the radial phase f and its C³ bounds. The linked condition instead concerns the origin correction g, its value g(0)=1 and its C² join to a constant.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: The Hermite representation uses two types of degrees of freedom: `node(k,p)` is a derivative of order $p$ at knot $k$, and `bubble(i,j)` is an interior coefficient on interval $i$.

anchor.heading: Splines and jets

comparisons.note: The two kinds of coefficient are nodal derivatives indexed by a knot and derivative order, and interior coefficients indexed by an interval and polynomial order.
The unit cardinal polynomial contains the factor xᵖ(1−x)ᴰ/p! and the finite binomial sum that imposes the required endpoint derivatives.
The left endpoint polynomial is (b−a)ᵖh((x−a)/(b−a)), so its derivative data use the physical coordinate x.
The right endpoint polynomial is (a−b)ᵖh((b−x)/(b−a)); its sign corrects the reversal of the interval coordinate.
The interior polynomial is ((x−a)(b−x))ᴰ(x−(a+b)/2)ʲ, providing the stated bubble coefficients after the endpoint derivatives are fixed.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: The constructor `JetSpline.toSpline` sums over the finite active degree-of-freedom sets, while its coefficient function is total on all pairs of degrees of freedom.

anchor.heading: Splines and jets

comparisons.note: The polynomial is reconstructed by a double sum over the two finite sets of active degrees of freedom, using a coefficient table defined on all pairs.
The active set contains derivative orders 0≤p<D at every knot and the prescribed finite set of interior orders on each interval.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: In `VanishesBeyond`, a missing knot defaults to the support radius, which makes the relevant guard true and forces the associated coefficient to be exactly zero.

anchor.heading: Splines and jets

comparisons.note: A missing knot is assigned the cutoff radius, so its vanishing condition applies and forces the corresponding coefficient to equal zero.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: `ScaledJetAxis.convert` fixes the orientation, signs, defaults and powers in this transformation.

anchor.heading: Splines and jets

comparisons.note: The conversion uses inverse powers of the nodal scales and the specified Jacobi coefficients, interval powers and bubble normalisations.
The ordinary coefficient table is obtained by applying the two one-dimensional conversion matrices to the scaled coefficient table.
The sentence describes the full scaled-jet conversion. This condition only checks the length and reflection symmetry of the node scales; it gives none of the conversion powers or signs.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: For integrals involving second derivatives, the reference-field route uses the specified `knotZeroHess` representative at spline seams.

anchor.heading: Splines and jets

comparisons.note: The specified Hessian equals zero on spline seams and equals the represented Hessian elsewhere, fixing the representative used by the reference-field calculation.
The reference-field condition identifies its supplied second derivative with that seam convention for the converted, joined spline data.

comparisons.note: The field formula evaluates affine amplitudes with a moving phase. Its affineness on the stated ball additionally needs the zero-phase consequence of the step-spline conditions.
The matching radius is Ls*/(1−s*), the physical radius corresponding to the step profile's interior edge.
The phase is defined by the stated radial integral. Its vanishing up to the matching radius requires the separate hypothesis that the step spline is exactly zero below its interior edge.

passages.quote: `IsStepProfile` specifies the joins, exact zero pieces and final constant branch of this phase.

anchor.heading: Parameter dependence, pressure and compact support

comparisons.note: The step spline has ordered knots, C² joins, an interior cutoff knot, exact zero pieces below it and a constant-one branch near one.
The theorem derives the regular radial phase and its vanishing in the matching region from the full step-spline conditions.

The pressure condition identifies the residual's pressure contribution with ∇(p−|Wᵃ|²/2) for every parameter vector.

anchor.heading: Parameter dependence, pressure and compact support

anchor.heading: Physical cells, row fields and matrices

comparisons.note: The computational mesh uses physical cylindrical rectangles and their harmonic and polynomial data, separate from the compactified meshes used by profile splines.
The radial reference coordinate is (2r−r₁−r₂)/(r₂−r₁), with derivative scale 2/(r₂−r₁).
The height reference coordinate is (2z−z₁−z₂)/(z₂−z₁), with derivative scale 2/(z₂−z₁).
The cell polynomial is evaluated in the two affine reference coordinates of its physical rectangle.

The sentence requires divergence-free polynomial triples. This formula chooses their Gram inverse-square-root mixing matrix and does not impose their divergence identity.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: In particular, one lower-bound constructor takes a minimum of the two chart values on the equator.

anchor.heading: Weights and potential fields

comparisons.note: On the equator the lower-bound value takes the minimum of the two chart values before applying the prescribed radial decay.
Away from the origin the chart bound uses that lower equatorial value and its radial factor; the origin has a separately supplied value.

passages.section: Data representation
passages.quote: For base azimuthal order $n=\kappa\iota_1$, the plus, minus and axial components have orders $n+1,n-1,n$.

The construction evaluates the four potential fields from the series. The normal-direction joins stated in the sentence are separate admissibility conditions on those series.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 1
passages.quote: The `cell` field supplies the geometric, analytic and finite-dimensional structure on which the multiplier and cell arguments operate.

anchor.heading: 1. cell: the cell problem and its common constants

comparisons.note: The first of the fifteen requirements supplies the common geometry, shapes, coefficients and finite-dimensional cell and tree assumptions used by B.1 and B.4–B.8.
The common cell assumptions fix the geometry and representations together with w=39/50, c=3/50, pin weight 1000 and row bound 400(1+2⁻¹⁸).
The uniformity condition fixes the reference profile, weight and coefficient data across the parameter set, with only the expressly allowed frame dependence.
The coefficient conditions give common lower bounds and mode coverage uniformly on their stated cells and exterior regions.
Each analytic leaf has a Hermitian 12×12 lower bound acting on the nine gradient and three velocity entries, together with derivative floors and charge bounds.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 2
passages.quote: The `shape_valueSets` field requires a positive period and constant positive weight, together with harmonic sets closed under the stated symmetries.

anchor.heading: 2. shape_valueSets: the values needed by the shape-to-analysis bridge

comparisons.note: The second requirement supplies positive periods on K, the fixed positive weight and the required harmonic support and symmetry conditions.
The seven conditions require positivity of the period throughout K, a fixed positive weight, harmonic symmetry closure, the zero harmonic and the required reference supports.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 3
passages.quote: The `entry_conditions` field ties the finite assembly matrices to the analytic cell forms, omitted modes and exterior estimates.

anchor.heading: 3. entry_conditions: the meaning of the assembled matrices

comparisons.note: The third requirement identifies the assembly matrices with the analytic cell forms and includes omitted-mode and exterior coverage.
The twenty assembly conditions connect the represented matrices to their analytic forms, permitted vectors, tail budgets, omitted modes, exterior covers and global coordinates.
The permitted vectors include the physical slaved coordinates, arbitrary allowed gauge and pressure shifts, and real coordinates in both actuator blocks.
The exterior conditions supply measurable covers, null overlaps and the appropriate pointwise or ray estimates with the same allocated charges.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 4
passages.quote: The `enclosure_numbers` field requires the same three numerical multiplier bounds to hold for every parameter in the certificate set.

anchor.heading: 4. enclosure_numbers: bind the multiplier bounds to this instance

comparisons.note: The fourth requirement imposes the selected multiplier enclosures for every parameter in K, using the same represented fields and numerical bounds.

For the supplied period and fields, the multiplier conditions bind the reference and frame bounds, positive frequency margins and the three selected numerical enclosures; the common cell condition requires these at every parameter in K.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 5
passages.quote: The `coerciveL2_ge` field requires the certificate's forcing coefficient to dominate the constant derived by the multiplier estimate.

anchor.heading: 5. coerciveL2_ge: the coefficient of the forcing norm

comparisons.note: The forcing coefficient must dominate √(((1+ε+ε′/√w)²/c)+b/cμ)/√c, with the constants supplied by the same cell instance.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 6
passages.quote: The `coercivePin_ge` field requires the certificate's pinning coefficient to be at least $\sqrt{1000/(3/50)}$.

anchor.heading: 6. coercivePin_ge: the coefficient of the pinning error

comparisons.note: The pin coefficient must dominate √(1000/(3/50)), exactly the fixed pin weight divided by the fixed coercivity under the square root.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 7
passages.quote: The `certificate` field contains the remaining numerical and parameter-inclusion conditions consumed by Theorem 7.1.

anchor.heading: 7. certificate: the numerical hypotheses used after coercivity

comparisons.note: The seventh requirement carries the remaining sign, norm, smallness and parameter-inclusion assumptions used by the certificate theorem.
The remaining certificate assumptions include the sign and norm bounds, three smallness inequalities, frame invertibility, parameter inclusions and strict nontriviality.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 8
passages.quote: The `instantiation` field identifies the certificate's profile, second derivatives, pressure gradient and adjoints with the specified shape constructions.

anchor.heading: 8. instantiation: identify the actual profile, pressure and adjoints

comparisons.note: The eighth requirement identifies the supplied profile, Hessian, corrected pressure and fixed adjoints with their validated representations.
The represented centre, tangent, pressure and adjoint fields are identified with the certificate data, including the profile pin target and the fixed adjoints of decay order at least three.
The profile condition identifies the represented field and Hessian for every parameter and sets the target equal to that profile's pin values.
The pressure condition identifies the residual's pressure contribution with ∇(p−|Wᵃ|²/2) for every parameter vector.
Each active adjoint is the same represented field for all parameters, with radial decay order at least three.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 9
passages.quote: The `offset_expansion` field checks the interior residual coefficients, their enclosure errors and the exterior Cauchy-Schwarz remainder used by Lemma B.13.

anchor.heading: 9. offset_expansion: certify the parameter polynomial and its tail

comparisons.note: The ninth requirement encloses the interior constant, linear and quadratic pairings and supplies the exterior L² product used in B.13.
The offset assumptions give affine reciprocal-period and multiplier formulas, absolute coefficient-error enclosures on the closed matching ball and nonnegative exterior norm budgets.
The diagonal coefficient contains one ordered quadratic term, while an off-diagonal coefficient contains the sum of both orders.
The offset budget adds the constant error, radius-weighted linear errors, one triangular quadratic sum and the product of the two exterior norm bounds.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 10
passages.quote: The `shift_numbers` field bounds the change from the frozen reference profile to the central approximate profile and then across the parameter set.

anchor.heading: 10. shift_numbers: move estimates from the reference field

comparisons.note: The tenth requirement gives the central and parameter discrepancy bounds with their distinct L² and L³ gradient norms.
The four nonnegative bounds control the central difference in the uniform and gradient L² norms and the parameter difference in the uniform and gradient L³ norms.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 11
passages.quote: The `frozen_form` field supplies a lower strain bound and an $L^3$ gradient bound for the frozen model.

anchor.heading: 11. frozen_form: control the frozen quadratic form

comparisons.note: The eleventh requirement gives the frozen reference strain lower bound and L³ gradient bound with their specified scalar budget.
The frozen-form assumptions combine a pointwise lower strain bound and a uniform L³ gradient bound with their specified weighted scalar cost.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 12
passages.quote: The `adjoint_quadratic` field turns an adjoint size bound into the coefficient of the quadratic perturbation term.

anchor.heading: 12. adjoint_quadratic: bound the nonlinear adjoint pairing

comparisons.note: The twelfth requirement chooses an L³ or L² adjoint estimate and compares its exact weight-dependent coefficient with the stored quadratic allowance.
For each active adjoint, one selected L³ or L² bound and its matching coefficient must fit within the certificate's quadratic adjoint allowance.
The size condition uses the spatial L³ norm in one branch and the spatial L² norm in the other.
The L³ coefficient is 2/(√3 w), while the L² coefficient is S(w)/√w with S(w)=[2π(2√w)]⁻¹ᐟ².

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 13
passages.quote: The `adjoint_links` field identifies the adjoint-defect calculation with the profile, adjoints, coupling matrix and reciprocal-period expansion already chosen.

anchor.heading: 13. adjoint_links: use the same fields in the defect calculation

comparisons.note: The thirteenth requirement binds the adjoint calculation to the same profile, coupling matrix and reciprocal-period formula, with no fitted directions.
The defect calculation uses the chosen adjoints, coupling coefficients, central and tangent fields and reciprocal period; its fitted-direction set is required to be empty.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 14
passages.quote: The `potential_entries` field supplies the shape-valid potentials and compact pin fields used in the adjoint defect identity.

anchor.heading: 14. potential_entries: construct admissible integration-by-parts fields

comparisons.note: The fourteenth requirement supplies the validated potential and compact pin representations and their exact identifications with the defect data.
The potential and pin assumptions validate their represented shapes and identify the resulting centre potentials and pin matrices with those used in the defect calculation.
The potential conditions require the stated endpoint alternatives and joins; for fluxes they require radial joins of the radial component and polar joins of the polar component.
The pin representation uses compactly supported divergence-free generators with the exact cutoff and spline conditions required by integration by parts.
The theorem derives weak derivatives and decay of the four potentials from their finite series conditions and the analytic facts about those series.

passages.section: CellSystemCondition field 15
passages.quote: The `adjoint_defect` field bounds the weak adjoint error after the potential decomposition, uniformly over the parameter set.

anchor.heading: 15. adjoint_defect: close the adjoint error budget

comparisons.note: The fifteenth requirement imposes the potential, free-direction, time-shift and pin budgets uniformly on K and bounds their total by the linear adjoint allowance.
The eighteen adjoint-error conditions bind the coordinate, potential, free-direction, time-shift and pin budgets and require their final sum to fit the certificate allowance.
The nonnegative potential budgets bound the period norms of G, ∇U and F, using Frobenius norms for the matrix quantities.
The dual bound is a decomposition into a finite azimuthal part and an ordinary weighted remainder, whose nonnegative budgets sum to at most the claimed bound.
The azimuthal bound requires measurable amplitudes, reconstruction, rotation covariance and distinct component/time/order triples, with weights 1/2,1/2,1 and denominator (|n|+1/2)².

Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.chartCoord.text: The radial variable is σ=|y|/(L+|y|). A period-one time variable elsewhere in the formulas is independent of this compactified radius.

Breakdown.CertCell.labelFlip.text: The lattice reflection is ι↦(−ι₁,ι₂−ι₁). Under (j,n)=(2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁), it becomes (j,n)↦(j,−n), preserving temporal frequency and reversing azimuthal frequency.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.text: The target is required to equal the pin values of the approximate profile for every parameter. Consequently the target gap in the generic certificate is identically zero for this cell construction.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsPotentialSeri.text: The radial flux joins across radial interfaces and the polar flux across polar interfaces. These normal-component joins supply the weak divergence used in integration by parts, while the permitted tangential jumps do not introduce additional surface terms.

Breakdown.CertReduction.AdjointSizeBound.text: The two alternatives bound the spatial $L^3$ or $L^2$ norm of the adjoint. The $L^2$ alternative pairs with the perturbation’s uniform-norm estimate and its constant $S(w^*)=[2\pi(2\sqrt{w^*})]^{-1/2}$.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.rows.text: The represented rows and their nonnegative weights are stored separately. Multiplying each row by the square root of its weight gives the paper’s seminorm [F]² as a sum of squared row pairings.

Breakdown.CertCell.labelHarmonic.text: A paper label ι corresponds to temporal frequency 2ι₂−ι₁ and azimuthal frequency κι₁. Every mode set and frequency-dependent coefficient must be read using this same conversion.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe.text: The positive and negative parts of each whole mode density and of the stretching term are integrated separately, allowing infinite positive integrals. Once the negative part is finite, the multiplier comparison also makes the positive part finite and permits the subtraction used in B.20.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.treeState_ho.text: Local moments and the corresponding global coordinates can differ by gauge and constant-pressure shifts. The cell forms are required to ignore those shifts, preserving their quadratic values for every allowed choice of free coordinates.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.patchGradSq.text: For azimuth k, the rectangle test-gradient energy is |∂rφ|²+|∂zφ|²+k²|φ|²/r². The last term is part of the Dirichlet bound even though the test polynomial is represented on the meridional rectangle.

Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.hessTailGain.text: The coefficient-tail norm and the physical energy with measure r dr dz have different radial factors. In the coefficient normalisation the Hessian gain is r* times the first omitted polynomial eigenvalue, plus (k₀−2)₊²/r₂, where r*=r₁ off the axis and r*=1 on an axis cell.

Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.pointwiseQua.text: A certified lower bound for the curl-gradient coefficient may be negative even though the actual coefficient is nonnegative. The scalar argument handles that case explicitly and also permits a zero diagonal in the final two-by-two quadratic test.

Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsDirectionR.text: A radius depending on direction must also be measurable, constant along positive rays and bounded between one positive lower bound and one finite upper bound. These are the geometric hypotheses used to extend the ray estimate to weak perturbations.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.complexCo.text: The real and imaginary contributions of a complex loss column are counted as two indexed real columns. They may be dependent or zero; their count still bounds the possible dimension lost to the negative squares.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.stateTerm.text: The finite-dimensional argument allows the prescribed coordinates to change by a fixed linear function of the free coordinates and removes the pressure coordinates ignored by the quadratic form. This gives the general version of the paper’s physical/free-coordinate decomposition.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.shiftValid_of_.text: There are exactly two discrepancy fields: the difference between the frozen and central profiles, and the displacement across the parameter set. Their gradient estimates use L² and L³, respectively, with the corresponding distinct constants.

Breakdown.CertReduction.adjointQuadCoeff.text: The $L^3$ adjoint bound has coefficient $2/(\sqrt{3}\,w^*)$. The $L^2$ adjoint bound uses the perturbation’s uniform estimate and has coefficient $S(w^*)/\sqrt{w^*}$, where $S(w^*)=[2\pi(2\sqrt{w^*})]^{-1/2}$.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded.text: The distinct label is the entire triple consisting of helical component, temporal frequency and azimuthal order. Amplitudes with the same triple must be added before taking their squared norm, so the budget retains their cross terms.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.RemainderDualBou.text: The dual conclusion records spatial integrability for almost every time and integrability of the resulting scalar time pairing. Joint absolute integrability follows from a separate weighted-norm argument after the finite harmonic amplitudes have been shown to supply a finite |y|R norm.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.PotentialData.text: The four fields represent the vectors Gⱼ and Uⱼ, the matrix for Fⱼᵀ and the scalar qⱼ. Derivative maps use output-component rows and differentiation-direction columns, so their matrices are transposed relative to the paper’s written gradient convention.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.PotentialNorms.text: The numerical budgets for ∇Uⱼ and Fⱼ use the Frobenius norm, whereas the analytic decay bounds use operator norms. A freely chosen decay constant can absorb norm equivalence; a fixed numerical budget must satisfy its specified norm bound.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.text: The pin flux uses the skew derivative of each compact pin generator. Its divergence agrees with the required pin Laplacian up to a gradient term, whose pairing with a divergence-free perturbation vanishes.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad.text: The general adjoint argument permits fitted directions with individual potentials. This cell construction requires that fitted set to be empty, leaving the centre potential and the free-direction terms of B.12.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Of.text: An off-diagonal quadratic coefficient already contains both ordered terms. The final sum runs only over i≤l, counting each off-diagonal pair and each diagonal term once.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.text: The finite frame is indexed by actuator first and adjoint second: its (l,j) entry is the coefficient of β_l in Vⱼ·β. The enclosures use a closed ball; changing to the paper’s open ball changes only a sphere of measure zero.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert.text: The newly chosen witness is a common decay bound. The certificate retains the supplied profile, period, multiplier, pins, adjoints, parameter family and numerical budgets.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe.text: B.1 is stated for the paper’s specialised data and a signed density integral. The formal theorem allows general symmetry data and explicit weak derivatives and compares the positive and negative nonnegative integrals; specialising the data and using finite negative part gives B.20.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.text: B.2 combines B.20 and B.21 with the stated numerical constants. The formal theorem starts from their combined multiplier inequality and allows general admissible constants; the same completion of the square gives B.2 after the cell specialisation.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeDensityBri.text: The formal reduction gives separate quarter-plane identities for the positive and negative mode densities and stretching terms, including the lattice and reflection conditions. With finite negative part these give the signed identity B.23 and also provide a defined formulation when the positive part is infinite.

Breakdown.CertCell.cellLayerParts_closed.text: The formal result assembles the analytic consequences of the full cell assumptions, including negative-part finiteness, exterior bounds and local comparisons. B.4 states these through its four correction terms; recovering that presentation uses the supplied matrix and entry conditions and supplies no concrete numerical entries.

Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.angularModeP.text: After converting a paper label to its temporal and azimuthal frequencies, the result is the four almost-everywhere curl and angular inequalities in B.35. It applies directly to the specified weak derivatives of the perturbation.

Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.pointwiseQua.text: The formal theorem is a scalar implication for nonnegative derivative sizes satisfying the four angular inequalities and the coefficient bounds. Substituting the actual mode sizes yields the pointwise nonnegativity test of B.5, including the case of a negative lower curl-gradient enclosure and a zero final diagonal.

Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeRayInver.text: The rewritten B.6 explicitly includes the formal assumptions that the directional radius is measurable, constant along positive rays and uniformly bounded above and away from zero. With those hypotheses the weak-mode inverse-square estimate has the same constant 1/4+(|k|−1)₊².

Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.exteriorCond.text: The formal result establishes the complete exterior tests from coefficient bounds, angular estimates and both ray and square inverse-square inequalities. The numbered B.6 is the ray case; the zero-azimuth square case uses the constant two from B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedTre.text: The formal lower bound retains the root-front quadratic form together with the pivot gains and loss-column squares. Dropping its nonnegative root term gives B.41, after the real or complex enclosure results have supplied the node inequalities.

Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed.text: The formal result derives the global row estimate from an explicit full list of cell, coverage, matrix and compatibility conditions. Printed B.8 relies on a partly unstated coefficient specification, so the resulting estimate agrees after the given identifications while equality of the complete hypothesis lists cannot be established from the paper alone.

Breakdown.CertReduction.gapTransferBridg.text: For the central and parameter discrepancy fields chosen by the cell construction, the theorem gives the convection-change estimate 7.19 used in B.9. It keeps the distinct L²-gradient and L³-gradient costs; the frozen-form estimate is a separate contribution.

Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge.text: For the frozen reference field, the theorem gives B.9’s lower form bound from the strain allowance and L³ gradient bound. The separate change-of-profile estimate supplies the remaining error in the final form constant.

Breakdown.CertReduction.formShiftBridge_.text: For the two chosen profile discrepancies, the theorem gives B.9’s change-of-form cost, including the factors $1/(2\sqrt{w^*})$ on the appropriate products. Adding the reference lower bound gives the stated final form bound.

Breakdown.CertReduction.adjointQuadratic.text: For the fixed adjoint selected by the cell data, the conclusion is B.10’s period-integrated quadratic pairing bound, with the same L³ and L² alternatives. The general theorem also allows a parameter-dependent adjoint satisfying the same bounds.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.dualBoundedBound.text: The formal theorem gives B.11’s dual norm inequality for weak-gradient tests on one period, without needing test periodicity. It records iterated integrability; the paper’s joint absolute-integrability claim is obtained from the separate weighted-norm estimate.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri.text: The cell specialisation gives the same linear adjoint budget as B.12, while the formal assumptions additionally specify weak potential derivatives, sharper Laplacian decay and a decaying curl potential for the test approximation. The full shape construction supplies these additional analytic requirements.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of.text: For the represented cell profile and its zero target gap, the theorem gives the offset estimate of B.13. The closed matching ball has the same integrals as the paper’s open ball, and the upper-triangular quadratic sum uses the same symmetrised coefficients.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert.text: The formal construction assumes fifteen explicit groups of conditions on the same supplied data and proves that they form a certificate after selecting a common decay bound. B.14 states the conditional certificate conclusion under a coefficient specification only partly printed, so the complete hypothesis formats cannot be identified from the paper alone.

Breakdown.CertCell.formNegFinite.text: The theorem proves finiteness of the negative quarter-plane form from uniform coefficient lower bounds and reference-field regularity, with general coercivity and without an equation involving the forcing or actuator coefficients. At c=3/50, the separate quarter-plane identity multiplies this form by 4π to give the finiteness of I⁻ used in B.4 and B.8.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.representationHo.text: This theorem proves the weak adjoint-pairing identity used in B.12, explicitly requiring the decaying curl potential and the solenoidal approximation argument. The subsequent potential, parameter and pin estimates provide the lemma’s final numerical error bound.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of.text: The theorem gives the almost-everywhere quadratic residual expansion inside the matching ball once the represented fields agree with their central-phase expressions there. Diagonal coefficients occur once and off-diagonal coefficients combine both orders; the coefficient enclosures and exterior norm product are separate hypotheses of the final offset estimate.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderAzimuth.text: The theorem proves the finite azimuthal component of B.11’s signed dual bound with the denominator (|n|+1/2)² and component weights 1/2,1/2,1. The full printed lemma also includes the ordinary remainder and joint absolute integrability, supplied by separate arguments.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.spaceBreakdown.text: B.14 concludes that the supplied data form a certificate. The formal theorem also applies the later certificate and profile implications to obtain conditional breakdown on space, while retaining the full hypothesis that the given cell data satisfy their conditions.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.weightedPairingI.text: The theorem establishes joint absolute integrability from weak-gradient energy and a finite weighted norm of the other field. It supplies the integrability step in B.11 after the amplitude argument establishes that weighted norm, and does not assert the sharper azimuthal dual constant.

Breakdown.CertReduction.adjointQuadTerm_.text: The theorem proves the almost-everywhere time-slice bound for the absolute quadratic adjoint integrand using the stated L² or L³ choice. B.10 concludes the period-integrated bound, obtained by the separate integration theorem.

topics.name: The blow-up statements
topics.description: Smooth solutions, breakdown on space and on the torus, and the theorems that state them (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1).

topics.name: The fractional extension
topics.description: The authors' separate extension with dissipation exponent between 1 and 5/4, outside the classical paper.

topics.name: Heat flow and mild solutions
topics.description: The heat semigroup, the bilinear Duhamel term, mild solutions, restarting and uniqueness (§3).

topics.name: Recurrent profiles
topics.description: Self-similar time-periodic profiles, their slices and orbits, and weak profiles read as physical fields (§2, §4.1, §7.11).

topics.name: Monodromy and the correction
topics.description: The period map, its compact-plus-small splitting, the spectral projection and the fixed point that corrects a profile to an exact solution (§4).

topics.name: Passing to the torus
topics.description: The solenoidal cutoff, periodization and the periodic right inverse that move the construction onto the torus (§5–6).

topics.name: From certificate to profile
topics.description: Certificate data, the free operator, convection, held solutions and the smoothing of the weak profile they produce (§7).

topics.name: The coercive multiplier estimate
topics.description: The multiplier, its five density coefficients and lower bound, and the a priori estimate it gives (Appendix B.1 and B.2).

topics.name: Encoded cell data
topics.description: The finitely represented inputs: coordinates and harmonics, the profile representation, splines and jets, physical cells, rows, weights and potentials.

topics.name: Reduction to the quarter plane
topics.description: Symmetry reduction of the density to the meridian quarter plane (B.3).

topics.name: Cells, traces and tails
topics.description: Integrability, the common vector of unknowns, resolved modes, the tail budget and the exterior estimate (B.4).

topics.name: Angular and ray-exterior tests
topics.description: The angular inequalities, the pointwise test and the integrated test on ray exteriors (B.5 and B.6).

topics.name: The matrix tree lower bound
topics.description: The tree conditions on the cell matrices and the passage from all cells to the global inequality (B.7 and B.8).

topics.name: Changing the profile
topics.description: Bounds for moving estimates from the reference field to the actual profile (B.9).

topics.name: The adjoint pairing and its error
topics.description: The quadratic adjoint pairing, the azimuthal dual norm and the linear adjoint error with potentials and pins (B.10 to B.12).

topics.name: The offset and the certificate
topics.description: Enclosing the constant, linear and quadratic offset, and the fifteen fields of CellSystemCondition that make the data a certificate (B.13 and B.14).
